# A Model for Shared Covariance

Factor analysis explains dependence among observed variables through a smaller
number of unobserved common factors. For experimental unit $i$, the Gaussian
common-factor model is

$$
\boxed{
\mathbf Y_i=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf F_i
+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i,
}
$$

with

$$
\operatorname{E}(\mathbf F_i)=\mathbf0,
\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf F_i)=\boldsymbol\Phi,
\quad
\operatorname{E}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i)=\mathbf0,
\quad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i)=\boldsymbol\Psi,
$$

and $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf F_i,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_i)=\mathbf0$.
Usually $\boldsymbol\Psi$ is diagonal, expressing local independence of observed
variables conditional on the factors. Marginally,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf Y_i)
=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}
+\boldsymbol\Psi.
}
$$

The loading $\lambda_{jk}$ describes how variable $j$ changes with factor $k$
on the chosen latent scale. The uniqueness $\psi_j$ is variable-specific
variance not explained by the common factors. When variables are standardized,
the communality is

$$
h_j^2=(\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi
\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T})_{jj},
\qquad
1=h_j^2+\psi_j.
$$

The model separates common and specific variation. This is a scientific and
statistical assumption, not a consequence of calculating eigenvectors.

# Exploratory and Confirmatory Questions

**Exploratory factor analysis (EFA)** searches for a low-dimensional loading
pattern with limited prior restrictions. Rotation is used to find an interpretable
representative among observationally equivalent or near-equivalent solutions.

**Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)** specifies a measurement model in advance:
which variables load on which factors, which residual associations are allowed,
and whether parameters are shared across groups. CFA can test implications of a
theory, but good fit does not prove that the named factors exist or that the model
is uniquely causal. Alternative latent structures can imply similar covariance.

The intended estimand should be explicit. Possible targets include the covariance
decomposition, a prespecified loading, a group difference on a defined latent
scale, or prediction of an external outcome. A fitted factor score for a person,
sample, or cell is an estimate under the model, not a directly observed trait.

# Identification, Scale, and Rotation

The representation is not unique. For any invertible matrix $\mathbf T$,

$$
\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf F_i
=\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf T
(\mathbf T^{-1}\mathbf F_i).
$$

Constraints are therefore needed to set the scale, orientation, and sometimes
rotation. Common choices fix factor variances to one or fix one loading per factor.
Changing every loading and factor score for one factor by $-1$ leaves the observed
distribution unchanged, so factor signs are arbitrary.

In an orthogonal factor model, $\boldsymbol\Phi=\mathbf I$ and rotations satisfy
$\mathbf T^{\mathsf T}\mathbf T=\mathbf I$. Oblique rotations permit correlated
factors and can be scientifically more plausible. Orthogonal rotation should not
be chosen merely because its plot is convenient: forcing independent factors can
redistribute loadings and obscure real factor correlation.

Identification requires enough nonredundant covariance information for the
free parameters and a loading pattern that fixes rotational ambiguity. Counting
parameters is necessary but not sufficient. Weak loadings, nearly indistinguishable
factors, too few indicators, or residual dependencies can make estimation unstable
even in a formally identified model. Inspect the information matrix, likelihood
profiles, convergence across starts, and sensitivity to constraints.

# Estimation and Uncertainty

Under multivariate normality, maximum likelihood compares the sample covariance
$\mathbf S$ with the model-implied covariance

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\theta)
=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\Phi\boldsymbol\Lambda^{\mathsf T}
+\boldsymbol\Psi.
$$

Apart from constants, the covariance part of the log-likelihood for $n$
independent units is

$$
\ell(\theta)
=-\frac n2\left[
\log|\boldsymbol\Sigma(\theta)|
+\operatorname{tr}\{\mathbf S\boldsymbol\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}\}
\right].
$$

Other estimators include principal-axis factoring, generalized or weighted least
squares, robust likelihoods, and Bayesian models. Ordinal indicators need models
for category probabilities or latent response variables rather than routine
Gaussian treatment. Count, binary, zero-inflated, or censored measurements require
observation models that respect their support.

Standard errors and likelihood-ratio tests rely on identification, independent
experimental units, and regularity conditions. Boundary estimates such as a
uniqueness near zero can invalidate routine approximations. Robust or sandwich
standard errors can address some nonnormality but do not repair a wrong factor
structure, dependence between rows, or selection of the model using the same
tests later reported as confirmatory.

In a Bayesian analysis,

$$
p(\boldsymbol\Lambda,\boldsymbol\Phi,\boldsymbol\Psi,
\mathbf F_{1:n}\mid\mathbf Y)
\propto
p(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf F,\boldsymbol\Lambda,\boldsymbol\Psi)
p(\mathbf F\mid\boldsymbol\Phi)p(\theta).
$$

Priors can regularize weak loadings and residual variances, but rotational and
sign symmetries still need attention. Posterior predictive checks should compare
observed and replicated covariances, marginal distributions, residual associations,
and group-specific patterns. Prior sensitivity is essential when the likelihood
weakly identifies a factor.

# How Many Factors?

Factor number is a modeling decision, not a mechanical reading of eigenvalues.
Useful evidence includes subject-matter theory, residual covariance, parallel
analysis, likelihood-based comparisons under their conditions, information
criteria, held-out prediction, and stability across samples.

A scree plot alone is ambiguous. The rule “retain eigenvalues greater than one”
depends on standardization and can over- or under-extract. Too few factors leave
structured residual covariance and can bias loadings. Too many create weak,
unstable factors that absorb noise or method artifacts. Decisions made through
exploration should be confirmed in independent data or clearly labeled exploratory.

# Factor Scores Are Predictions, Not Measurements

Even with known parameters, $\mathbf F_i$ is latent. Regression scores use a
conditional mean such as $E(\mathbf F_i\mid\mathbf Y_i)$; Bartlett scores use a
weighted residual criterion. Different scoring rules need not agree, and factor
scores can be indeterminate because many latent values are compatible with the
same observed covariance model.

Using estimated scores in a downstream regression as if error-free ignores both
score uncertainty and estimated measurement parameters. This can attenuate or
otherwise distort associations and understate standard errors. Prefer a joint
model for measurement and outcome when the downstream coefficient is the target,
or propagate uncertainty through multiple plausible scores or posterior draws.

# Model Checking and Sensitivity

Global fit indices compress many discrepancies and should not replace targeted
checks. With large samples, trivial deviations can be statistically detectable;
with small samples, serious misspecification may escape detection.

| Assumption or risk | Why it matters | Evidence and response |
|---|---|---|
| Correct factor number | determines the covariance rank attributed to common causes | inspect residual covariance, stability, theory, and held-out fit |
| Local independence | diagonal $\boldsymbol\Psi$ rules out residual dependence | examine residual correlations; add only scientifically justified residual links |
| Stable measurement | loadings and intercepts define the latent scale | test and estimate plausible invariance patterns across groups or time |
| Appropriate observation model | Gaussian likelihood may mishandle counts, categories, tails, or censoring | use generalized factor models or robust likelihoods |
| Independent units | row dependence changes likelihood information | model donor, family, time, plate, or spatial clustering |
| No influential units | covariance is sensitive to extremes | inspect case influence and robust sensitivity analyses |
| Identified factors | otherwise parameters and scores are arbitrary or unstable | inspect rank, profiles, starts, constraints, and posterior geometry |

Modification indices are diagnostic prompts, not automatic instructions. Adding
the largest suggested cross-loading or residual covariance repeatedly capitalizes
on chance and changes the model's meaning. Any revision should have a substantive
rationale and be evaluated in new data.

# Measurement Invariance and Group Comparisons

Comparing latent means across conditions requires the indicators to define the
factor comparably. In a common sequence:

1. **Configural invariance:** the broad loading pattern is shared.
2. **Metric invariance:** corresponding loadings are equal, supporting comparison
   of factor relationships on a common unit.
3. **Scalar invariance:** intercepts or thresholds are equal, supporting latent
   mean comparisons.
4. **Residual invariance:** uniquenesses are equal, a stronger condition needed
   for some reliability or observed-score comparisons.

These levels are modeling conventions and should be evaluated through effect
sizes, residuals, uncertainty, and scientific consequences, not a rigid sequence
of thresholded tests. Partial invariance can be defensible if noninvariant
parameters are identified transparently and the latent scale remains anchored.

# Bioinformatics Example: A Gene-expression Program

Suppose a prespecified panel of genes is measured in tumors from independently
sampled patients. A factor model may represent a shared expression program, while
gene-specific uniqueness includes measurement noise and biological regulation
not shared by the panel. Patients are the experimental units. Reads, technical
libraries, repeated wells, and multiple sections from one tumor are not additional
independent patients; their dependence belongs in the measurement or multilevel
structure.

Design should balance biological condition across processing batches and include
enough independent patients to estimate covariance rather than relying on the
large number of genes or reads. Expression preprocessing must address library
size and mean--variance relationships. Fitting a Gaussian factor model to raw
counts gives a covariance decomposition on an inappropriate scale.

Statistically, a treatment-associated latent mean difference is conditional on
the chosen genes, loading constraints, measurement invariance, observation model,
and sampling design. Biologically, calling the factor pathway activation requires
coherent loadings, external annotation or perturbation evidence, reproducibility
across patients, and exclusion of plausible batch or cell-composition explanations.
A convenient rotated axis is not itself a molecular mechanism.

# Factor Analysis Compared with PCA

| Feature | Factor analysis | [Principal component analysis](principal-component-analysis.qmd) |
|---|---|---|
| Primary goal | model common covariance through latent variables | summarize total variance and reconstruct data |
| Representation | $\Sigma=\Lambda\Phi\Lambda^{\mathsf T}+\Psi$ | eigendecomposition of covariance or SVD of centered data |
| Variable-specific error | explicit uniqueness $\Psi$ | included in total variance |
| Scores | predictions of latent quantities | exact linear combinations after fitting |
| Identification | needs scale and rotation constraints | axes identified up to sign, and rotations within tied eigenspaces |
| Inferential basis | requires a probability model | algebra is distribution-free; inference adds assumptions |

PCA can initialize or inform exploration, but its loadings are not maximum-
likelihood factor loadings and its retained components need not estimate common
factors. Choose the method from the scientific target, not from superficial
similarity of biplots.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Latent-variable models](latent-variable-models.qmd) gives the general
  marginalization, identification, and score-uncertainty framework.
- [Normal and multivariate normal distributions](../probability-randomness/normal-and-multivariate-normal-distributions.qmd)
  supplies the Gaussian covariance model used in classical factor analysis.
- [Identifiability and label switching](identifiability-and-label-switching.qmd)
  separates structural nonidentification from weak empirical information.
- [Posterior predictive checks](posterior-predictive-checks.qmd) explains how to
  test model implications through replicated observed data.
- [Partial pooling and exchangeability](partial-pooling-and-exchangeability.qmd)
  is relevant when factor models contain group-specific parameters.

Factor analysis is a latent measurement model for shared covariance, not merely
a dimension-reduction algorithm. Interpretation depends on the observation
model, identification constraints, rotation, factor number, local independence,
and measurement invariance. Factor scores remain uncertain predictions. In
bioinformatics, independent biological units and external evidence are required
before a fitted factor can support population or mechanistic claims.
